Ch. 1: 'morituræ mustæ' is read as 'moriturae muscae', 'dying flies' (cf. Eccles. 10:1), and 'peccatores... non dabunt' seems to echo Ps. 140:5. 'ejus m(??)un sacrata tuba' is damaged; 'munere' (by his gift) is conjectured. 'hacteaus' is read as 'hactenus'; the sense 'thus far' is awkward. Ch. 3: the Donatist's sentence on the two baptisms seems corrupt. '(??)tendit' is taken as 'ostendit/extendit', and 'ejus pie meritum' may stand for 'vitae meritum' (cf. the Catholic's reply). Ch. 4: 'quies iguis' is read as 'quia ignis', and 'Fæta' as 'Facta'. 'in alia spe' is translated as printed; the Vulgate has 'in excelsis'. Ch. 5: the quotation is attributed to Ezekiel but cited from Isaiah 22.

Line 12: 'Deo-par Salomonem: probante' read as 'Deo per Salomonem probante'. Line 13: 'bo(??)(??)(??)r corpus' read as 'bonum corpus'; 'quin foris est' read as 'quia foris est'; the sentence about the Manichaean seems to say the opposite of what the argument requires (perhaps a negative has dropped out, 'non ... potandus est'), translated as printed. Line 18: 'Interpretes malo desuper' is obscure, perhaps for 'interpretaris male de super[biis]'; rendered tentatively. Proverbs reference printed as xvii, 6 is Prov. 27:6. Line 17: 'Isai. xlii, 26' corrected to 43:26.

Line 24: 'male, bene' carries a footnote mark in the edition; the sense appears to be that wherever water is named in a bad sense, the Donatist took it as Baptism in a good sense. 'Joannes et Mambres' are the magicians Jannes and Jambres (here in the Latin form Mambres). Line 25: the second half ('vel in abruptum ... abrepto charybdis vidit, et exterminii oleum ... animavit') is syntactically broken and probably corrupt (footnote marks after 'vel' and 'abrepto'); the translation is tentative. Line 32: 'in luo' read as 'in tuo'; 'nob(??)s' read as 'nobis'.

Line 39: the passage seems disordered; the sentence 'For because I do not approve yours...' and the 'Catholic replied' that follows read as if displaced, and the speakers are hard to follow; translated as given. Line 39 'recurum' read as 'securum', 'peragal' as 'peragat'. Lines 43–44: 'ejus' ('his [church]') is obscure, perhaps referring to the rival schismatic or the 'pirate' of line 39; possibly corrupt. Line 46 'retinxit' (re-dipped) refers to rebaptism. Line 48: 'Quomodo alter esse concessum?' is defective; read as 'alteri esse concessum'. 'Acts of Marcellinus' presumably refers to the proceedings of the Conference of Carthage (411), presided over by the tribune Marcellinus.

Line 57: 'ceram positum' read as 'coram positum' (present in person). Line 59 is badly damaged in the scan; the biblical citations (Mark 1:24, Acts 13:11, 1 Tim 1:20, Acts 5, Ps 17:38-39) have been restored from the evident text, and the names Elymas, Hymenaeus, Ananias and Sapphira from the cited passages. The words about Simon Magus are partly illegible. 'credo tamen quod mei facere potuerim' is uncertain; it is rendered as 'my people could have done it'. Line 61: 'ordinem virorum' is uncertain, perhaps 'ordinum' or 'honoratorum virorum'; it is rendered 'men of rank'. Line 64: 'adduxit' is perhaps for 'abduxit'. 'cognito ululatu suo' is odd but stands twice; it is rendered literally. 'Video quod fieri non potest' introduces ironic concessions. 'per tinctionem' means dipping, i.e. rebaptism.

nodes.text: A BOOK BY AN UNCERTAIN AUTHOR AGAINST FULGENTIUS THE DONATIST.

CHAPTER ONE. — The little book which your Reverence, brother Fulgentius, sent me, I have received without disdain; whether you composed it yourself or sought it from elsewhere, I do not much wonder. For this too is the duty of our religion: not to look to persons, but to seek the truth in all things, to acknowledge it when found, and to guard it when acknowledged. For so the apostle Paul says: Test all things, hold fast what is good; abstain from every evil appearance (1 Thess. 5:21, 22). I will therefore state briefly what you have spread out rather ingeniously in your letter. You said that there is one Baptism, which the Samaritan, that is, the heretic, has not deserved to have; that the one garden enclosed, which is the Church, has a fountain sealed, which no outsider touches; that there is one oil, which is the most holy chrism, which dying flies spoil, and which sinners will by no means give. Against these things a reply must be prepared by me with the Lord's help, and it must be taken from nowhere else but from the divine reading. Let us therefore now take the beginning of the Word, or rather let us hold to the Word himself, the beginning, the Lord Jesus, the leader and prince of the heavenly army; let us wage war, and with the trumpet consecrated by his [gift] let us assail the mighty walls of the wicked city of Jericho: that is, let us surround the height of worldly wisdom with the Lord's testaments, let us sound out with voices of truth and freedom; let us compel the adversaries to take refuge, because of the destruction of the world, in the house of Rahab, that is, of the Church which received his messengers; let us condemn the obstinate with anathema, so that we may thus far be victors. These things, then, you have taken up at the very outset, as a strong barrier, from the Law against the Law, from God's Testament against God's Testament, from the fountain of truth against the fountain of truth, as if truth could be defeated by itself, or the glory of light be darkened by its own light.

CHAPTER II. The Donatist said: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, the teacher and guardian of the one Baptism, so that error of mind might not lead thirsting souls away through dry cisterns, proclaiming that the everlasting draughts are his own, bore witness thus in his Gospel, saying: Whoever thirsts, let him come and drink; whoever believes in me, as Isaiah says.
The Catholic replied: It does not have 'as Isaiah says', but 'as Scripture says'. But I will pass over such things as hindrances, so as not to shut out the reader's profit with a long discourse.

The Donatist said: Whoever believes in me, as Isaiah says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly (John 7:37, 38); and so that it might not be said that one can drink anywhere and everywhere, he himself distinguished the merits of the waters, when he condemned the origin of Samaria's apostasy at its own well. Whoever drinks, he says, of this water will thirst again; whoever drinks of the water that I shall give will not thirst for ever, but there will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life (John 4:13).

The Catholic replied: You certainly set these things down so as to show us Catholics to be like Samaritans and without Baptism. Now then, begin to look upon the Donatists in the Samaritans. The doctrine of the Samaritans, as the book of Kingdoms teaches, was this: they feared God, and at the same time worshipped images; they kept the divine law, and by no means abandoned the errors of their fathers; they had the sign of circumcision, and did not hold to the fellowship of the Israelites (3 Kgs 12 and 13). You do this too: you fear God, and you likewise worship a clay image, Donatus. For he too was fashioned from the dust of the earth. You keep the divine law, and do not abandon the error of your parents; you have the sacrament of Baptism, and you do not wish to have communion with the Catholics. See, you resemble them in all things. As, then, the circumcision of the Samaritans could not then be given a second time, so now the Baptism of the Donatists ought not to be repeated, since the Lord Christ says, Whoever has been washed once has no need to be washed again (John 13:10). For the circumcision of the Samaritans signifies the Baptism of the Donatists, as the Apostle says, You were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping off of the body of the flesh, but in the circumcision of Christ, buried with him in Baptism (Col. 2:11, 12). But when the Lord says, Whoever drinks of this water will thirst again, he spoke not of Baptism but of the earthly element. For if he had wished to point to Baptism here, he would by no means have asked [for it] from the Samaritan woman. Finally, that well was called not Samaria's but Jacob's, and Jacob certainly was not a heretic, but beloved of God, ever dear, and he himself drank from it, and his sons, and his cattle.

CHAPTER III. The Donatist said: The spirit of the Church therefore never suffers to be joined [to it] what has deserved to be denounced by the divine mouth, as the proclamation of the Law forewarns: Two against two, one against one (Ecclus. 33:15). And the Lord in the Gospel: Then, he says, two will be in the field; one will be taken and one left; two women grinding at the mill; one will be taken and one left (Matt. 24:40, 41). You see, then, that there are two kinds of baptisms and two rewards of merits: the one is burned up by the heat of a deadly nature, and the heat of a drinking thirst boils away the everlasting draughts; the other, which once for all has ordained everlasting life through the channels of thirsts to be quenched, certainly [shows] perpetual drynesses in dug-out pools, and when it has closed off its merit, it has opened the way to death, as Jeremiah says: This people has done two evils: they have forsaken me, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns, which cannot hold water (Jer. 2:13). And again: All who forsake you will be confounded; those who withdraw from you will be written in the book of death, because they have forsaken you, the fountain of life (Jer. 17:13).

The Catholic replied: You [assert] one against one; I assert many baptisms against one. For the pagan baptizes, and the Jew baptizes, and the Sadducee baptizes, and many outside the rule of the given law do not cease to baptize. But that one is the one which is true, that is true which is Christ's, that is Christ's which is of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; this is true, this saving, to this nothing is to be compared. Whoever does not receive this has himself both closed off for himself the merit of life and opened the way to death.

CHAPTER IV. The Donatist said: But if, as you assert, one faith subsists in both, why did he distinguish by a just separation between faithful water and faithless, as the Lord testifies through Isaiah: Who has told you that fire burns? Who has told you of that eternal place? He who walks in righteousness, proclaims the right way, hates crime and injustice, and keeps his hands from gifts, and stops his ear so as not to hear the judgment of blood, and shuts his eyes so that they may not see iniquity, he will dwell in another hope; strong bread will be given him, and his water [will be] faithful (Isa. 33:14-16). Separating faithlessness from its faith, he set it down thus, as Jeremiah testifies: Why do those who wrong me prevail? My wound has become solid; whence shall I be healed? It has become to me like lying water that has no faithfulness (Jer. 15:18).

The Catholic replied: All heretics, although they disagree among themselves in their own reasoning, yet agree in the solemn wording in the handing on of Baptism: just as circumcision was one, but subsisted with differing faith among the Jews and the Samaritans of old. It is necessary, therefore, that as then, so now it must be done for converts, that what is sought by reasoning alone should in turn be undone by reasoning alone; so that they may hear from the Lord: You are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you; abide in me and I in you (John 15:3). For all these things happened to them in figure; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. 10:11).

CHAPTER V. — The Donatist said: Ezekiel also spoke thus: And they will see that there are many who have turned away the water of the ancient pool, and have not looked to him who made it from the beginning, and have not seen him who founded it (Isa. 22, according to the Septuagint). Unheard-of madness of the faithless, neither to be willing to believe the divine words, nor to be willing to save the Apostle's simple teaching from the jaws of their error.

The Catholic replied: Far be it, far be it from us to draw off the water of the ancient pool to a party, as you do, or not to believe the divine utterances. What we read, we believe; and what we believe, we preach. Hear what our origin is, and where its water has been spread abroad. In Zechariah you have it thus: Living waters will go out from Jerusalem, half of them to the eastern sea, and half of them to the last sea; that is, from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth; they will be in summer and in winter; that is, they will be at every time. And the Lord will be king over all the earth (Zech. 14:8, 9): that is, Christ will rule over all the earth, not Donatus. This is the possession, this the inheritance of Christ, which is tilled by the saints and watered by an everlasting fountain, of which it was said to him, I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession (Ps. 2:8). Whoever is in it is enrolled as an heir; whoever is not in it is already condemned and destined to death, as Scripture says, Whoever goes out of the doors of your house will be guilty against himself (Exod. 12).

CHAPTER VI. — The Donatist said: Hence God proclaims that for him Baptism is unique; hence the Apostle confirms that he said to all that it is one; God proving it through Solomon: A garden enclosed, my sister, my bride, a fountain sealed, a well of living water, a paradise with the fruit of apples (Song 4:12, 13).

The Catholic replied: Recall, read everything, attend carefully and see that from this paradise, from this enclosed garden, from this sealed fountain, the wave of salvation runs down even outside, which goes against the Assyrians, that is, against you Donatists. For from the Assyrians are born those Samaritans who have been compared to you. This, says Scripture, is the river that goes against the Assyrians (Gen. 2:14); against the nation hostile to the people of God; it goes not for them but against [them]. For to some it is the odour of death unto death, but to others the odour of life unto life (2 Cor. 2:16). For just as he who eats and drinks the blood of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgement to himself (1 Cor. 11:29), so also he who receives Baptism unworthily receives judgement, not salvation. For Judas the betrayer too received the good body [of Christ], and Simon Magus the good Baptism of Christ; but because they did not use the good well, being evil they were destroyed by using it evilly. Baptism is good, the blood and body of Christ are good, the law is good, but if one uses it lawfully (1 Tim. 1:8). Nor, because it is outside, is it therefore not divine; or, because it is held by strangers, will it be thought to belong to strangers; or, because it is unjustly handled by the wicked, will it be justly condemned by us. The water of paradise is the water of the Trinity: where we recognise this, we do not deny it is of paradise; where we do not discern it, we do not call it of paradise at all; whatever has arisen outside is in no way to be called of paradise: for instance the Manichaean, since he was never in paradise, nor went out from the Church as you did, must be given the water of paradise to drink, because he arose outside. He needs it in order to live, lest he die for ever; but in order to live lawfully, let him live in it, lest he eat and drink judgement.

CHAPTER VII. — The Donatist said: On the contrary, the Apostle bears witness that he said: One God, one faith, one Baptism (Eph. 4:5). There is no variation in divine teaching; in all things the servant follows the Lord, in nothing does the disciple differ from the Master. Whom do you follow, whom do you imitate, whom do you judge to be the author of this outrage?

The Catholic replied: Give me any one of the saints who rebaptised after [baptism in] the Trinity, as you do. Read me, not those writings by whose authority I am not bound, but [those] of the New and Old Testament, to which we are both subject. If Baptism is true, why do you double what is one? For you repeat nothing other than what you find to be true. Since, therefore, you build up again the things you destroyed, you show yourselves to be transgressors.

CHAPTER VIII. — The Donatist said: Or if you think the sacrament of Baptism is one even when joined by some mixture with the guilty, hear the Prophets, to whom it is rightly assigned, as Solomon says: The fountain of life is in the hands of the just (Prov. 10, according to the Septuagint).

The Catholic replied: Well did the Lord, who foresaw your error, say of you: You are those who justify yourselves before men; but the Lord knows your hearts; for what is lofty among men is abominable before God (Luke 16:15). If you are just, and the fountain of life is in your hand, you are not a man but God. Let people take refuge in you, let them believe in you, let all hope of life be placed in you, let Baptism itself be given in your name, and let the Lord be passed over in silence. Do you wish to know where to seek this fountain of life? In the Psalm you have it: With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light (Ps. 35:10). Have you not read: A wicked son has proud eyes; a wicked son calls himself just, but does not wash away his goings out (Prov. 24, according to the Septuagint)? Unless you recognise that you, as a man, are guilty, unless you cry out with a truthful heart that you are a sinner, you cannot be justified at all, as the prophet says: Tell your iniquities first, that you may be justified (Isa. 43:26). And John the apostle: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us (1 John 1:8). CHAPTER IX. — The Donatist said: And David says: But let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head.

The Catholic replied: Name me, then, any one of yours whom you can prove not to be a sinner, so that your oil cannot be a sinner's; since it is written, There is no man who does not sin (Eccles. 7:21). You interpret wrongly from above. Read, so that you may grasp the sense: it says thus, The just man will correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head (Ps. 140:5): that is, a merciful rebuke is better than gentle flattery; as also this: Better are the wounds of a friend than the willing kisses of an enemy (Prov. 27:6). The oil of the sinner is the blandishment of the flatterer, of whom it says elsewhere: His words are softer than oil, and they are darts (Ps. 54:22). The oil of the just is the Spirit of God, as Peter says: Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit (Acts 10:38). Cease, therefore, to call the Holy Spirit the oil of a sinner, lest you begin to assert that God is a sinner.

CHAPTER X. — The Donatist said: In this place is shown the open confession of the faithless, which is polluted when touched with hostile presumption by a criminal priest, whose sacrifice, like the oil, is rejected by the divine voice. The criminal, it says, who sacrifices to me is like one who kills a dog; and he who offers fine flour, like pig's blood; and he who offers incense as a memorial, like a blasphemer (Isa. 66:3).

The Catholic replied: It is certain that God curses and despises the burnt offerings of priest and people if a good conscience is not present. Or if you want it understood as said of priests alone, how is it that among you the consecration of criminal priests is not polluted? You say: As long as the wicked are hidden, they cannot defile; because it is written, "What is hidden is mine; what is manifest is yours" (Deut. 29:29). If, then, as long as the wicked are hidden they cannot defile, why do you not fear to rebaptise far-off nations, to whom the name of Donatus and Caecilian is unknown? Which of you ever brought the misdeeds of any to their knowledge? And even if he had brought it and not proved it, it would harm not at all, according to this: What is hidden is mine; what is manifest is yours.

CHAPTER XI. — The Donatist said: Further, the Prophet in spirit reveals its muddied waters: You set your horses on the sea, it says, troubling many waters (Hab. 3:15). The city of Gilead, which works folly, has despised me; it troubles the waters; and your strength is like that of a pirate (Hos. 6:8, 9).

The Catholic replied: Recognise that your own weapons are turned against you, as it is written: Let their sword enter into their own hearts, and let their bow be broken (Ps. 36:15). Your strength, Donatist, is like that of a pirate; you who rebaptise by force, fight by force in the water, kill by force in the water: doing these things, you will be captured and killed as a pirate, unless you are converted and repent, and serve as a soldier for Christ the king in the Catholic [Church].

CHAPTER XII. — The Donatist said: If, then, the Church glories in a single fountain, surely that is the den of the traitors which exalts itself in a multitude of waters, and, confounded by the drunkenness of its Baptism, commits fornication with kings, as John says: Come, I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot who sits upon many waters, and all who dwell on the earth have been made drunk with the wine of her fornication (Rev. 17:1). I ask, what are the many waters, if not many baptisms? What is the fornicating woman, if not the den of the traitors, which serves, subject, the pleasures of kings, from whom, drinking the cup of persecutions, she mixes [it] for the peoples in drunken blindness and leads into madness those whom she has watered? Access to her the most wise Solomon forbade: Keep yourself, he says, from strange water, and do not drink from a strange fountain, that you may live a long time, and the years of your life may be added to you (Prov. 9:18, according to the Septuagint). Let the fountain of your water be your own, and let no stranger share it with you (Prov. 5:16, 17). So only she has no private fountain who possesses the harlot's multitude of waters. John the apostle too condemns the multitude of waters, saying: And the angel said to me, The waters which you saw, on which that harlot sits, are peoples, multitudes and nations (Rev. 17:15).

The Catholic replied: As I see it, wherever water is named in a bad sense, you took [it] to be Baptism in a good sense. But you wanted to assign it to yourself in the good sense and to me in the bad, so that what the apostle Paul said might be fulfilled in you: Understanding neither what they say nor the things about which they make assertions (1 Tim. 1:7). For as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these resist the truth (2 Tim. 3:8). The angel says: The waters which you saw are peoples, multitudes and nations. And you resist the angel who explains [it], and say: I ask, what are the many waters, if not many baptisms? What is the fornicating woman, if not the den of the traitors? If you want to learn the names of the traitors as well, you have your own: Silvanus of Cirta, handing over the Sacraments to Felix the curator. You have Marinus of Aquae Tibilitanae, offering three books to the Roman curator. You have Victor of Rusicade, burning the four Gospels as if they were worthless, who dared to condemn Caecilian, innocent and absent. This is the den of thieves, this the offspring of the traitors, this the fornicating woman who has left Christ and opened her brothel to Donatus: whose house, according to Solomon, is a retreat of death, whose ways are the ways of the underworld (Prov. 7:27); who calls herself clean when she is full of filth; who proclaims herself innocent when she is entangled in crimes; who commits shameful acts and attributes her deeds to another, so that she may not be the first to hear what she has committed. For you defame Catholics with your own deeds, in order to separate the peoples from the Lord. Again, as for your urging those you regard as yours to keep away from our water, saying: Keep yourself from strange water, and do not drink from a strange fountain; let the fountain of your water be your own, and let no stranger share it with you: who does not see that the Prophet was commending chastity to married people, and that you have strayed far from the truth? Or if no stranger ought to share your fountain, why do you seek strangers, why do you rebaptise Catholics?

CHAPTER XIII. — The Donatist said: It is clear, then, that among the traitors there is a multitude of waters, where [there are] diverse seeds of schisms, where the manifold plagues of heretics, where the detestable dregs of the filth of the Manichaeans, or [where] Charybdis has seen [them] snatched down into the steep pool of a muddy whirlpool in eternal death, and has kindled the oil of destruction with devouring flames.

The Catholic replied: O what proving! O what straying! O what raving! It is clear, then, that among the traitors there is a multitude of waters, where [there are] diverse seeds of schisms, where the manifold plagues of heretics, where the detestable dregs of the filth of the Manichaeans: how do you prove that the manifold plagues of schismatics are with us? If they were with us, they would not be heretics but catholics.

CHAPTER XIV. — The Donatist said: Hear Solomon saying: Dying flies destroy the preparation of sweetness (Eccles. 10:1). The sweetness, then, is natural to the oil, and if it has been violated by a wicked touch, it becomes unpleasant, polluted in its preparation. And rightly do you traitors make the Holy Spirit equal to unclean winged creatures, because you wickedly fall upon another's table and foul the sweetness of the oil with unclean touches.

The Catholic replied: Who violates with a wicked touch: he who preserves what he finds, or he who shamelessly destroys what has been prepared? When did we touch your oil, when did we drive away the Holy Spirit by doing [him] injury? Show that any one of us has wickedly fallen into the oil of the Godhead, or has unlawfully violated the Baptism of the Trinity, as you do. The dying flies, the Donatists, fly around through the members of the whole body, to find any place that is wounded; they sting the healthy, they lick the sick, and into their sores they pour the worms of sins, which gnaw the conscience, which make an end of the soul, which feed the rot, which do not spare even dead corpses. Dying flies, when they destroy the oil, are killed by the oil: for you do not live, you who breathe out the Holy Spirit.

CHAPTER XV. — The Donatist said: This the most holy David, supplying the rule of our faith, properly teaches: that the oil of a sinner neither brings salvation nor ought to touch anyone's head. Let not the oil of the sinner, he says, anoint my head (Ps. 140:5). Therefore the person of the sinner must be sought out by careful examination, if the Lord did not speak of a sacrilegious priest, as the profane assert.

The Catholic replied: Though you are conscious of sin, you dare to say: The person of the sinner must be sought out. Hear who this person of the sinner is. The Apostle said: For all have sinned, and lack the glory of God (Rom. 3:23). And Solomon: There is no one among men who does not sin (Eccles. 7:21). And Job: In his angels he found perversity; how much more in the sons of men, who have an earthly dwelling (Job 4:18, 19)? This is the person of the sinner: that is, every man is a sinner. If you are a priest, you are a man; and if you are a man, you are a sinner. What do you make yourself? You have said that you alone are holy, you alone just, you alone without sin, you alone without stain. You have said that Baptism is yours, the holy oil yours, the Lord's table yours, all those things yours which are divinely granted to the faithful. What remains, except that you wickedly and impiously declare yourself to be God? But hear what the head of pride deserved to hear: How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, you who rose in the morning, who wounded the nations, who said in your heart: I will ascend above heaven, and above the stars of God I will exalt my throne, I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, in the sides of the north, and I will be like the Most High? But you will go down into hell, and into the depth of the pit (Isa. 14:12-15). Unless, then, you repent, unless you are converted, unless you lay aside pride and ask pardon for your sins, you will hear what he did too; because, though you are a man, you make yourself God.

CHAPTER XVI. — The Donatist said: Likewise the Lord through the prophet Haggai showed, by a wholesome exposition, that unclean touches confer defilement, and that no polluted person can sanctify, if with unlawful presumption he tries to touch what he sees to be held holy, when he set forth the Prophet as a caution for us. Ask the priests, says the Lord, saying: If a man binds holy flesh in the hem of his garment, and the hem of the garment touches any created thing of bread, or of wine, or of oil, is it sanctified? And the priests answered and said: No. And the Lord said: If one unclean in soul touches any of these, will it be defiled? And the priests said: It will be defiled. And the Lord said: So too is this people, and so is this nation: everyone who approaches there will be defiled (Hag. 2:12-15).

The Catholic replied: You have used this testimony against yourself, you who put the gift of God in your own power of decision. For if the touch of the holy does not remove the defilements of the unclean, vain is what is done, what you consecrate, what you wash. If, it says, it touches what is holy, a created thing of bread, or of wine, or of oil, will it be sanctified? And the priests answered and said: No. Where is that for which you exalt yourselves, your boast that your holiness confers cleanness? Or if you are moved by what it says, So is this people, and so is this nation; everyone who approaches there will be defiled: show that Haggai, who said these things, went out from the midst of that same people so that he himself would not also be polluted among them. That touch signifies works. If a holy man, it says, touches the unclean, it will not be sanctified; if an unclean man touches the holy, it will be defiled: that is, a holy man who has been joined to this most wicked nation is more easily made wicked than this nation is changed for the better; because one runs more readily to imitate the wicked than the mind is roused to the virtues of the good: just as a little wormwood thrown into a great deal of honey quickly draws bitterness, but even if twice as much honey is thrown in [to the wormwood], its sweetness cannot be obtained. We must therefore go out from the midst of the wicked in mind, not in flesh; in works, not in bodies. Do not, says the Apostle, share in the unfruitful works of darkness (Eph. 5:11): works, he says, not altars. For it is written in Isaiah: Those who say, Go away from me, do not come near me, because you are unclean; these will be smoke in my anger, a fire burning all day (Isa. 65:5). If the words of men do not frighten you, let at least the anger of God who threatens turn you back.

CHAPTER XVII. — The Donatist said: Never has a robber brought his plunder out into the light; always the workers of the night have shuddered at the light that is welcome to all the good: only the traitor is not broken by the threats of God, and wickedly glories in another's garment. Against him the Lord cries out through Zephaniah, and is not heard: It will be, he says, on the day of the Lord's sacrifice, and I will take vengeance on the princes, and on all who are clothed in another's garment (Zeph. 1:8).

The Catholic replied: I do not fear your accusations, because my conscience is secure. The one you say made the handing over, show the name and place of the traitor. You will never be able to show it, just as you were not able before. But even if you produce someone, he will not be able to harm me, since the Lord says: The soul of the father is mine; the soul of the son is mine; the soul that has sinned, it alone will die (Ezek. 18:4). I, however, do not rejoice in another's garment, I who always exult in the catholic faith. That is the [garment] I have, with which the merciful and kind Father clothed me in beauty on the day of redemption. Bring, he says, that first robe, and put it on him: because this son of mine was dead, and has come to life again; he was lost, and has been found (Luke 15:22, 24). That one, surely, of which the apostle Paul said: As many of you as have been baptised in Christ have put on Christ (Gal. 3:27). This I have, in this I rejoice, in this I will always appear more glorious. This is the one which you have either taken away like robbers, or, wretched men, defile.

CHAPTER XVIII. — The Donatist said: For inasmuch as wickedness longs to build its straying errors onto the goods of others, and tries to cover its false catholic [claim] with clouds of lying, it walks along winding hills; and the Lord met it as an opponent through Jeremiah: Do not, he says, trust in yourselves with false words, because they will not profit you in anything, saying, The temple of the Lord, it is the temple of the Lord (Jer. 7:4). And the Lord in Deuteronomy: Take heed to yourself that you do not offer burnt offerings in every place that you see; but in the place which the Lord your God will choose in your tribe, there you will offer burnt offerings, and there you will do all that I command you today (Deut. 12:13, 14).

The Catholic replied: Excellent, and very fitting for your salvation is the testimony you have put forward: Take heed to yourself that you do not offer burnt offerings in every place that you see; but in the place which the Lord your God will choose in your tribe, there you are to offer burnt offerings, and there you will do all that he will command you. Hear, then, which is the chosen place, and which the tribe of the Lord that was foretold. In the hundred and thirty-first Psalm you have: For the Lord has chosen Zion, he has chosen it as a dwelling for himself. This is my rest for ever and ever; here I will dwell, because I have preferred it. Likewise in the hundred and twenty-first Psalm: Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem. Jerusalem, which is built as a city. For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, a testimony to Israel. This is the chosen place, this the sanctified mountain, this the city set on a mountain so that it cannot be hidden, this the catholic root, this the fruitful vine spread far and wide, which cries out in Ecclesiasticus and says: In Zion I was founded, and in Jerusalem is my power (Ecclus. 24:15). For it was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:46, 47). You would rightly rebuke me if you remained in this inheritance. But since you do not remain in this inheritance of God the Father, and do not serve as a soldier in this tribe of Christ the King, why do you, a deserter, reprove a soldier? Why do you, a guilty man, upbraid the innocent? And I say to you: Take heed to yourself that you do not offer in every place, that is, in every heresy, and say, God is here too, and God is there: but in the place which the Lord your God will choose in your tribe, that is, in his tribe, there you will offer your burnt offerings, and there you will do all that has been commanded you. Do this, and you will live.

CHAPTER XIX. — The Donatist said: That certainly cannot be called Baptism which a throng of waters has scattered, which malice has separated from the font of the Church, which a barren wave has dried up, which has seen neither an angel, nor found a prophet who could heal it; as in the fourth book of Kingdoms the most holy Elisha, driving out death, healed the deadly waters, and with a fertilising word allowed them to flow into rich offspring. And the men of the city said to Elisha: See, the situation of the city is good, as you yourself, lord, see; but the waters here are many and barren. And Elisha said: Bring me a new earthenware vessel, and put salt into it. And they brought it: and he came to the springs of the waters, and threw in the salt and said: Thus says the Lord, I have healed these waters, and there will be no death in them, nor barrenness: and the waters were healed to this day (4 Kgs. 2:19-22).

The Catholic replied: Thanks be to God the Father, who, faithful, has fulfilled in us what he showed would come. Thanks, I say, to God the Father, who sent to us not angels only, not prophets, as formerly to our Jericho, that is, into this world, but his own Son, namely the Lord of the angels and the prince of the prophets, so that, driving out death, he might heal the barrenness of the waters, that is, the unfruitfulness of the nations. He took an earthenware vessel, that is, a body of human frailty; he put in salt, that is, he filled it with divine wisdom; he threw it into the water, that is, he went down into the Jordan; he healed the waters by his descent, that is, he redeemed the nations by his coming; and with a fertilising word he gathered the Church from the nations, and spread it far and wide into rich offspring. Whoever does not see this fulfilled in us is blind; whoever does not believe it is mad. Look at the rich offspring: say where this Church is not; say where yours is found, except in a corner of Africa, badly gathered, like a useless vine-shoot: from this [vine] where it was cut off, there it has stayed; it could not spread further, because, cut off from the root, it at once withered.

CHAPTER XX. — The Donatist said: One city received the substance of saving water; one widow with her children received the gift of oil; nor did the prophet entrust the divine favour indiscriminately, but only to her whom he knew to have one vessel of oil, as the truth of Kingdoms proves: And a woman, one of the wives of the prophets, cried out after Elisha, saying: Your servant my husband is dead; and you know how your servant feared the Lord: and see, those to whom I owe [money] have come to take my two sons as slaves. And Elisha said: What shall I do? Tell me, what do you have in your house? And she said: I, your handmaid, have nothing in the house except one vessel of oil. And Elisha said: Go, ask for vessels from outside, from all who live near you, many vessels; and you will go in, and shut the door upon yourself and your sons, and you will fill the vessels with oil, and you will pay the debt (4 Kgs. 4:1-4). For Elisha worked through the outlines of true Baptism. For because I do not approve yours, I therefore exsufflate [i.e. breathe out upon, in exorcism] your faithful. The Catholic replied: For all do this which you also do; all exsufflate the faithful, while they claim for themselves the single sacrament of Baptism. When you find such a one, you will not catch him, you will not hold him, you will not bind him with this chain: but, recognising the pirate's sign, you let him go away unharmed, so that he may carry on the trade with you.
CHAPTER XXI. — Fulgentius said: Far be it from me to let him go away, since God said: Compel all to come in, so that my house may be filled (Luke 14:23). He who said all, excepted no one.
Augustine replied: What then will you do? Fulgentius said: I will teach him that my church is most certain.
Augustine replied: On what [ground]? Will you show that Christ, who received all nations from the Father, has remained only in an African fragment?

Fulgentius said: I will say that it consists in few. Augustine replied: What if his [church] too will have few? For all, in comparison with the Catholic [Church], have few. Fulgentius said: I will show that that is the true [church] which suffers persecution, not that which inflicts it.
Augustine replied: What if his [church] too has inflicted no persecution at all?
Fulgentius said: I will point out, according to the Apostle, that my Church alone has no wrinkles and spots (Eph. 5:27).

Augustine replied: It will at once be proved to have them. For it is written: No one is clean from filth, not even if his life on earth has been of one day (Job 14:4, 5). But why say more? By what device will you catch and hold [him]? How do you receive one who has perhaps re-dipped your faithful, who has extinguished the Holy Spirit in the heart of the believer?
CHAPTER XXII. — Fulgentius said: I bind him, I exsufflate him, and I baptise him with true water for the forgiveness of sins.

Augustine replied: How do you forgive his sins, when it is written that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit cannot be forgiven for ever (Matt. 12:32)? But let us leave this one and look at another. Say also to the Maximianist, your rival, what you said to me: How can another have [it], if it has been granted to me alone? Or if you claim it has been handed over into your right, why do you approve another's? This Maximianist too will answer: How [can it] have been granted to another? For you received my Christians and clergy, baptised or ordained outside your Church, entire, without any change of Baptism or of rank; and when this was put to you in the Acts of Marcellinus, you were in no way able to refute it.
Again Augustine replied: If you are just, why is your judgement inconsistent? Why do you receive the Maximianists, and exsufflate my faithful?
Fulgentius said: Because he was mine. Augustine replied: And you were mine; why do you persist in being merciful to your schismatic, and merciless and implacable to the catholic?
CHAPTER XXIII. — Fulgentius said: You sinned more, and therefore vengeance is taken on you differently.

Augustine replied: What then, do you set Baptism down as a punishment, and is what is promised for salvation dealt out by you as a penalty? If in Baptism you do not pardon offences but chastise sins; if in the water you do not set free but scourge, you openly show yourself to be a pirate: and yet, how did I sin more? What did I do?
Fulgentius said: You handed over the books, and you sacrificed to idols. Augustine replied: Prove it; I did not do it, you are pinning your own deeds on me.
Fulgentius said: Your father did it.
Augustine replied: I know no father but God. For it is written: Do not call anyone your father on earth; for one is your Father, the heavenly one (Matthew xxiii, 9).
Fulgentius said: By your father I mean Caecilian: he handed over [the books], he offered incense, he committed every evil.

Augustine replied: Read who accused him, who convicted him, who condemned him when he was present. Suppose he did what he did not do: will the son be condemned for the father, when it is written: The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine; the soul that has sinned, it alone shall die (Ezekiel xviii, 4)?
Fulgentius said: You, his son, did not indeed hand over [the books], but you carried out a persecution against us.

Augustine replied: I indeed did not do it; yet I believe that my people could have done it. Look for the reason why: what if you deserved it? It is not a sin to persecute the wicked; for we read that both the saints and the Holy of holies, the Lord, persecuted the wicked. For the demons, unable to bear the Lord's persecution, cried out: What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come to destroy us (Mark i, 24)? And Paul [said to] Elymas: Behold, you will be blind (Acts xiii, 11), and [he handed] Hymenaeus [and Alexander] over to Satan (1 Timothy i, 20). And Peter killed Ananias and Sapphira his wife as liars (Acts v, 1-10): and he persecuted Simon Magus [...] so as to destroy him. And David too exults in the person of Christ and says: I will pursue my enemies and overtake them; and I will not turn back until they fail: I will afflict them, and they will not be able to stand (Psalm xvii, 38, 39). Not everyone, therefore, who has suffered persecution is at once to be thought just: but he who has suffered for the sake of justice, he truly is blessed, as Peter says: For what glory is it, if when you sin and are beaten you endure it? But if when you do well you suffer, and bear it patiently, this is grace with God (1 Peter ii, 20).
CHAPTER XXIV. — Fulgentius said: The saints you mention did not obtain edicts from secular judges, as your people did.

Augustine replied: Is it lawful, or is it not lawful? If it is lawful, it is not fitting to grumble about what is lawful: if it is not lawful, amend your own crime while you may. For you persecuted the Maximianists, your own schismatics, as the records declare, with the authority of secular judges, with the support of men of rank, and with the enforcement of various soldiers, after appointing defenders of the church, so as to drive them from their basilicas. You who rebuke me, why do you not first amend yourself?
CHAPTER XXV. — Fulgentius said: We took the basilicas from our schismatics in order to restore them to the true Church.

Augustine replied: Our people did this to you too: they took [them] from their schismatics and restored [them] to the Catholic mother. What your people did for the peace of Donatus, our people did for the peace of the body of Christ.

CHAPTER XXVI. — Fulgentius said: You are the schismatics, who both offered incense and handed over the books. Augustine replied: Let us become weak to the weak, that we may win the weak. I [grant what] I see cannot happen: the party of Donatus has conquered the whole body of Christ; an African corner has shut out the whole world; one nation has drawn away all the nations; the cutting has outgrown the vine, and has cut off the branches of the trees. At least you might keep the laws your predecessors laid down concerning us: not rebaptise, but free the souls of those who, as you think, are in error, through penance. Read again the decisions of your fathers, and see what they decreed ought to be done about traitors, those who offered incense, and schismatics, when they had come to Carthage in conspiracy against Caecilian. Your Marcianus among others gave such a sentence, which the seventy who were present certainly did not disapprove, saying: In his Gospel, he said, the Lord says: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman: every branch in me that does not bear fruit he will cut off and throw away; and every one that abides in me and bears fruit, he will prune it" (John xv, 1, 2). Therefore, just as fruitless branches are cut off and thrown away, so those who offered incense, the traitors, and those who are ordained in schism by traitors cannot remain in the Church of God, unless, having acknowledged their lamentation, they are reconciled through penance. Hence one ought not to be in communion with Caecilian, who was ordained in schism by traitors. This is the fixed sentence of your fathers. See: suppose, God forbid, we handed over, we offered incense, we committed schisms; why do you transgress the command of the elders in order to establish your own traditions? Just as fruitless branches, he says, are cut off and thrown away, so those who offered incense, the traitors, and those of us ordained in schism by traitors cannot remain in the Church of God, unless, having acknowledged their lamentation, they are reconciled through penance: through penance, not through dipping. If you please, let at least your own leaders overcome you: either confirm their decrees and lay aside your own inventions; or, if you want your own statutes to stand, declare that they erred. With us truth reigns; why is your tradition at odds with itself? The Saviour says thus in the Gospel: Every kingdom divided against itself will not stand, but will be laid waste (Matthew xii, 25).
